Learning to Couple: Context-Adaptive Joint
Denoising for Diffusion Language Models

Zilei Shao Ian Li11footnotemark: 1  Heng Zhao Kewei Lian Guy Van den Broeck Zhe Zeng Anji Liu University of California, Los Angeles University of California, San Diego University of Virginia National University of Singapore ††thanks: Equal contribution.††thanks: Corresponding author.
Abstract

Diffusion language models accelerate generation by predicting multiple tokens in parallel, but factorized denoisers treat simultaneous predictions as conditionally independent. Decoding heuristics reduce the resulting errors by controlling which tokens are committed, but leave the underlying distribution factorized. Joint modeling addresses the source of the problem, yet existing methods attach separately learned layers to frozen denoisers, leaving the backbone unadapted to the joint objective and the coupling parameters fixed across contexts. We propose Codpula, a context-parameterized denoiser combining a Transformer with a tractable probabilistic inference layer. Given a partially masked input, the Transformer produces token potentials that shape per-position predictions and compact gates that modulate the layer’s coupling parameters, yielding a context-dependent joint distribution while retaining exact conditional inference. We jointly optimize both components under a conditional denoising objective using a dual-flow multiplicative update that preserves valid probabilistic parameters. At inference, Codpula supports standard heuristics and uses conditional queries to adapt commitments to dependencies among proposed tokens without extra Transformer evaluations within a step. Codpula sets new state-of-the-art results across a broad suite of reasoning benchmarks while advancing the accuracy–latency Pareto frontier in mathematical reasoning and code generation.

1 Introduction

Masked diffusion language models can accelerate generation by predicting multiple tokens in parallel, reducing the number of denoising steps. However, standard denoisers factorize their predictions across positions (Austin et al., 2021a; Sahoo et al., 2024; Nie et al., 2025). Even under a shared context, these predictions remain conditionally independent, preventing the model from expressing dependencies among tokens predicted together. These missing dependencies become increasingly consequential as more tokens are committed at once (Liu et al., 2025a). A parallel denoiser must therefore predict both what each token could be and how its predictions depend on one another.

Many approaches address the factorization barrier during decoding by varying commitments, prioritizing confident predictions, or revising earlier tokens (Arriola et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025; Ben-Hamu et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2024; Israel et al., 2025). These methods improve the quality–computation trade-off while retaining a factorized denoiser. Joint modeling instead captures dependencies among simultaneous predictions (Li et al., 2026; Kim and Sung, 2026). Existing models, however, typically attach a separately trained joint layer to a frozen backbone. This layer produces context-dependent probabilities, but its dependency parameters remain fixed across inputs and the backbone is not optimized through the joint distribution.

We propose Codpula, a jointly learned, context-parameterized denoiser that adapts both token predictions and their coupling to the current context. From the backbone representation, Codpula derives token scores that adjust per-position predictions and a compact set of gates that reweight shared coupling parameters. The resulting joint distribution can favor different combinations of token values depending on the context, as illustrated in Figure 1 (left): Codpula assigns high probability to different combinations of sort direction and index for different requested operations. Training through this distribution teaches the backbone to produce token preferences and coupling signals that together explain the clean completion. To support this training, we derive a dual-flow update that accommodates the signed learning statistics introduced by conditional normalization while preserving valid probabilistic parameters.

Beyond modeling which token values belong together, the learned joint distribution informs which proposals to commit together. Codpula supports the token-selection heuristics used by existing block and full-sequence decoders and provides conditional queries for dependence-adaptive decoding. These queries measure how each proposal’s probability changes when the other candidates are assigned their proposed values. The decoder defers sensitive proposals, adapting the number of commitments to their dependencies. All queries reuse the token potentials and gates from the same Transformer forward pass, requiring no additional backbone evaluation within the step.

We evaluate Codpula on mathematical reasoning and code generation across four modern diffusion language models against a comprehensive suite of state-of-the-art baselines. The results show improved accuracy across a range of parallel decoding budgets and improved accuracy-latency trade-offs after accounting for inference overhead. Figure 1 (Right) highlights that Codpula achieves comparable accuracy with 2.95×2.95\times faster generation on AIME24 using LLaDA-2.0 and 4.02×4.02\times faster generation on MBPP using Dream.

2 Preliminary

2.1 Diffusion Language Models

Diffusion language models (dLLMs) learn to generate text from partially masked input by iteratively reconstructing masked portions of an input sequence (Austin et al., 2021a; Sahoo et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024). Let 𝒙0=(x00,…,x0L)∈𝒱L\bm{x}_{0}=(x_{0}^{0},\ldots,x_{0}^{L})\in\mathcal{V}^{L} denote a clean sequence, where 𝒱\mathcal{V} is a vocabulary. At timestep tt, each token is independently masked with probability αt\alpha_{t}, yielding a partially masked sequence 𝒙t=(xt0,…,xtL)\bm{x}_{t}=(x_{t}^{0},\dots,x_{t}^{L}). Given the partially masked sequence 𝒙t\bm{x}_{t}, a neural denoiser parameterized by 𝝋\bm{\varphi} predicts the original clean sequence 𝒙0\bm{x}_{0} using a factorized conditional distribution

p𝝋​(𝒙0|𝒙t)=∏i=1Lp𝝋​(x0i|𝒙t).p_{\bm{\varphi}}(\bm{x}_{0}|\bm{x}_{t})=\prod_{i=1}^{L}p_{\bm{\varphi}}(x_{0}^{i}|\bm{x}_{t}). (1)

Under this factorization, the denoising objective evaluates reconstruction only at masked positions, leaving the observed tokens unchanged. To construct a training example, we sample a clean sequence 𝒙0∼pdata\bm{x}_{0}\sim p_{\mathrm{data}} and a timestep tt, then obtain 𝒙t\bm{x}_{t} by independently masking each token in 𝒙0\bm{x}_{0} with probability αt∈(0,1]\alpha_{t}\in(0,1]. The model is trained by maximizing the weighted denoising objective

ℒ⁡(𝝋)=𝔼t,𝒙0,𝒙t​[w⁡(t)​log⁡p𝝋​(𝒙0|𝒙t)],\mathcal{L}(\bm{\varphi})=\mathbb{E}_{t,\bm{x}_{0},\bm{x}_{t}}\!\left[w(t)\log p_{\bm{\varphi}}(\bm{x}_{0}|\bm{x}_{t})\right], (2)

where 𝒙0∼pdata\bm{x}_{0}\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}, and w⁡(t)w(t) is a weighting function (Sahoo et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024).

At inference, generation starts from a fully masked sequence and progressively reveals tokens as tt decreases. With enough denoising steps, the model can reveal one token at a time, allowing every prediction to condition on all earlier ones. In this sequential limit, Equation 1 represents the desired target distribution since only one token is predicted at each step. In practice, however, fast generation requires revealing multiple tokens per denoising step. Equation 1 treats these tokens as conditionally independent, even though they may remain strongly dependent given the observed context. The model is thus asked to predict a joint completion using a product of token-wise distributions, which can produce inconsistent outputs (Xu et al., 2025a). Even perfectly learned token marginals cannot generally recover a dependent conditional joint distribution through their product, so increasing backbone capacity alone does not remove this representational constraint (Liu et al., 2025a; Hayakawa et al., 2025). Revealing fewer tokens per step can reduce the resulting dependence error, but requires more backbone evaluations (Ben-Hamu et al., 2025). We refer to this tension between parallel generation and factorized prediction as the factorization barrier (Li et al., 2026).

2.2 Parallel Denoising is Conditional Joint Prediction

Two broad approaches address the factorization barrier. The first retains the factorized outputs and compensates at inference. Heuristic-based decoding ranks positions by confidence, entropy, or margin (Chang et al., 2022; Ye et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2025); adaptive parallel decoding adjusts the number of tokens committed per step (Israel et al., 2025); remasking enables revision of previously generated tokens (Wang et al., 2025). However, tokenwise scores do not explicitly measure dependencies among jointly proposed tokens (Wu et al., 2025), while iterative refinement can trade additional model evaluations for improved sample quality (Zhao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025).

The second approach confronts the barrier directly by modeling the conditional joint distribution of tokens predicted in parallel. Coupled Discrete Diffusion (CoDD) (Li et al., 2026) and tensor-train joint modeling (Kim and Sung, 2026) use structured joint parameterizations to capture token dependencies while supporting efficient inference. Both approaches combine neural token potentials with a coupling model for simultaneous predictions. Their joint distributions can be expressed as

p𝝋,𝝎​(𝒙0|𝒙t)=1Z⁡(𝒙t)⋅p𝝎​(𝒙0|𝒙t)⋅∏i=1Lp𝝋​(x0i|xt).p_{\bm{\varphi},\bm{\omega}}(\bm{x}_{0}|\bm{x}_{t})=\frac{1}{Z(\bm{x}_{t})}\cdot p_{\bm{\omega}}(\bm{x}_{0}|\bm{x}_{t})\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{L}p_{\bm{\varphi}}(x_{0}^{i}|x_{t}). (3)

3 From Static to Context-Dependent Coupling

Equation 3 reveals a limitation of existing joint predictors. The dLLM’s tokenwise predictions p𝝋​(𝒙0i∣𝒙t)p_{\bm{\varphi}}(\bm{x}_{0}^{i}\mid\bm{x}_{t}) adapt to context, whereas coupling parameters 𝝎\bm{\omega} are fixed across inputs, mask patterns, and timesteps. A single coupling model must therefore capture dependencies in every denoising context, despite substantial variation in masked-token dependencies with the observed tokens.

The remedy is clear: token predictions and their dependencies must both adapt to the denoising context. We therefore propose the following context-dependent joint denoiser:

𝜽t=f𝝋​(𝒙t),p𝝋,𝝎​(𝒙0∣𝒙t):=p⁡(𝒙0,𝜽t,𝝎),\bm{\theta}_{t}=f_{\bm{\varphi}}(\bm{x}_{t}),\qquad p_{\bm{\varphi},\bm{\omega}}(\bm{x}_{0}\mid\bm{x}_{t}):=p(\bm{x}_{0};\bm{\theta}_{t},\bm{\omega}), (4)

where 𝜽t\bm{\theta}_{t} contains both the tokenwise prediction parameters and the context-dependent coupling parameters, while 𝝎\bm{\omega} denotes the parameters intrinsic to the probabilistic model.

There are many ways to parameterize p⁡(𝒙0,𝜽t,𝝎)p(\bm{x}_{0};\bm{\theta}_{t},\bm{\omega}), but the distribution must remain efficiently normalizable when 𝜽t\bm{\theta}_{t} changes with 𝒙t\bm{x}_{t}. To make this requirement explicit, we write

p⁡(𝒙0,𝜽t,𝝎)=p~​(𝒙0,𝜽t,𝝎)Z⁡(𝜽t,𝝎),Z⁡(𝜽t,𝝎)=∑𝒙0p~​(𝒙0,𝜽t,𝝎),\displaystyle p(\bm{x}_{0};\bm{\theta}_{t},\bm{\omega})=\frac{\tilde{p}(\bm{x}_{0};\bm{\theta}_{t},\bm{\omega})}{Z(\bm{\theta}_{t},\bm{\omega})},\qquad Z(\bm{\theta}_{t},\bm{\omega})=\sum_{\bm{x}_{0}}\tilde{p}(\bm{x}_{0};\bm{\theta}_{t},\bm{\omega}), (5)

where p~\tilde{p} is an unnormalized joint probability. Because 𝜽t\bm{\theta}_{t} changes at every denoising step, Z⁡(𝜽t,𝝎)Z(\bm{\theta}_{t},\bm{\omega}) must be recomputed for each 𝒙t\bm{x}_{t} and generally requires summing over exponentially many sequences. To overcome this challenge, we parameterize p~\tilde{p} using a probabilistic circuit (PC) (Choi et al., 2020), whose sum-product structure enables exact and efficient computation of Z⁡(𝜽t,𝝎)Z(\bm{\theta}_{t},\bm{\omega}) for dynamically generated 𝜽t\bm{\theta}_{t}. We next review background on PCs that make this computation tractable.

Probabilistic Circuits.

A probabilistic circuit (PC) represents a joint distribution through a rooted directed acyclic graph of input, sum, and product nodes (Choi et al., 2020; Poon and Domingos, 2011). Input nodes define univariate distributions over variables X∈𝑿X\in\bm{X}. Sum and product nodes recursively combine these distributions into a joint distribution over 𝑿\bm{X}. Formally, each node computes

pn​(𝒙)={gn​(𝒙),n​ is an input node over ​X∈𝑿,∏c∈𝖼𝗁⁡(n)pc​(𝒙),n​ is a product node,∑c∈𝖼𝗁⁡(n)𝝎n,c⋅pc​(𝒙),n​ is a sum node,p_{n}(\bm{x})=\begin{cases}g_{n}(\bm{x}),&n\text{ is an input node over }X\in\bm{X},\\ \prod_{c\in\mathsf{ch}(n)}p_{c}(\bm{x}),&n\text{ is a product node},\\ \sum_{c\in\mathsf{ch}(n)}\bm{\omega}_{n,c}\cdot p_{c}(\bm{x}),&n\text{ is a sum node},\end{cases} (6)

where 𝖼𝗁⁡(n)\mathsf{ch}(n) denotes the children of nn, gng_{n} is a univariate distribution over X∈𝑿X\in\bm{X}, and the nonnegative sum node parameters {𝝎n,c}n,c\{\bm{\omega}_{n,c}\}_{n,c} satisfy ∑c∈𝖼𝗁⁡(n)𝝎n,c=1\sum_{c\in\mathsf{ch}(n)}\bm{\omega}_{n,c}=1 (∀ sum node ​n\forall\text{~sum~node~}n). The key advantage of PCs is their ability to compute many probabilistic queries exactly and efficiently (Vergari et al., 2021). This tractability makes them particularly well suited to our setting: when p~​(𝒙0,𝜽t,𝝎)\tilde{p}(\bm{x}_{0};\bm{\theta}_{t},\bm{\omega}) is represented by a PC satisfying suitable structural requirements, the normalization constant (ZZ) in Equation 5 can be computed exactly in a single bottom-up pass.11 1 Appendix F.1 describes the specific structural properties of PCs and details of this bottom-up pass.

We next turn to training this hybrid denoiser. Applying the standard diffusion-ELBO derivation (Sahoo et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024) in this setting yields the following generalized denoising objective (see Appendix E, which we maximize jointly over the neural and circuit parameters):

ℒ⁡(𝝎,𝝋)=𝔼t,𝒙0,𝒙t​[w⁡(t)​log⁡p𝝋,𝝎​(𝒙0|𝒙t)],\mathcal{L}(\bm{\omega},\bm{\varphi})=\mathbb{E}_{t,\bm{x}_{0},\bm{x}_{t}}\!\left[w(t)\log p_{\bm{\varphi},\bm{\omega}}(\bm{x}_{0}|\bm{x}_{t})\right], (7)

where t∼𝒰⁡(0,1)t\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1), 𝒙0∼pdata\bm{x}_{0}\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}, 𝒙t∼qt(⋅|𝒙0)\bm{x}_{t}\sim q_{t}(\cdot|\bm{x}_{0}), and w⁡(t)≥0w(t)\geq 0 is the diffusion weighting function.

Although Equation 7 is differentiable end to end, its parameter blocks require different optimization treatments. The neural parameters (𝝋\bm{\varphi}) can be updated using standard gradient-based optimizers. The circuit parameters (𝝎\bm{\omega}), however, require expectation-maximization-style (EM-style) updates, whose constraint-preserving behavior relies on nonnegative log-parameter derivatives (Peharz et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2025b). While this condition holds for standalone PCs, the gradients induced by our objective can be signed, so the standard EM-style update does not apply directly. To make this issue precise, we first recall a general formulation that encompasses commonly used EM-style updates:

𝝎n,cnew∝𝝎n,c+α⋅T𝝋,𝝎​(n,c)⋅∂ℒ⁡(𝝎,𝝋)∂log⁡𝝎n,c,\bm{\omega}^{\mathrm{new}}_{n,c}\propto\bm{\omega}_{n,c}+\alpha\cdot T_{\bm{\varphi},\bm{\omega}}(n,c)\cdot\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}(\bm{\omega},\bm{\varphi})}{\partial\log\bm{\omega}_{n,c}}, (8)

where α≥0\alpha\geq 0 is the base learning rate, and T𝝋,𝝎​(n,c)T_{\bm{\varphi},\bm{\omega}}(n,c) is an optional per-parameter step-size multiplier. Varying the batch, α\alpha, and T𝝋,𝝎T_{\bm{\varphi},\bm{\omega}} recover full-batch EM, mini-batch EM, and Anemone (Liu et al., 2025b) as special cases (Appendix F.2 gives the correspondence). For standalone PCs, the derivatives in Equation 8 are nonnegative, so the normalized update preserves nonnegative weights.

Differentiating the normalized model in Equation 5 reveals why Equation 8 does not apply directly. For directly parameterized sum weights, holding the neural outputs and circuit inputs fixed, let F𝒙+​(n,c):=∂log⁡p~​(𝒙0,𝜽t,𝝎)/∂log⁡𝝎n,cF_{\bm{x}}^{+}(n,c):=\partial\log\tilde{p}(\bm{x}_{0};\bm{\theta}_{t},\bm{\omega})/\partial\log\bm{\omega}_{n,c} and F𝒙−​(n,c):=∂log⁡Z⁡(𝜽t,𝝎)/∂log⁡𝝎n,cF_{\bm{x}}^{-}(n,c):=\partial\log Z(\bm{\theta}_{t},\bm{\omega})/\partial\log\bm{\omega}_{n,c}. Then

∂log⁡p𝝋,𝝎​(𝒙0∣𝒙t)∂log⁡𝝎n,c=F𝒙+​(n,c)−F𝒙−​(n,c).\displaystyle\frac{\partial\log p_{\bm{\varphi},\bm{\omega}}(\bm{x}_{0}\mid\bm{x}_{t})}{\partial\log\bm{\omega}_{n,c}}=F_{\bm{x}}^{+}(n,c)-F_{\bm{x}}^{-}(n,c).

By construction, both Fx+​(n,c)F_{x}^{+}(n,c) and Fx−​(n,c)F_{x}^{-}(n,c) are nonnegative because the circuit computes p~\tilde{p} and ZZ using only additions and multiplications of nonnegative values; their derivatives with respect to log⁡𝝎n,c\log\bm{\omega}_{n,c} are therefore nonnegative as well. Their difference, however, can be negative. Consequently, directly applying Equation 8 no longer guarantees nonnegative circuit weights. To address this problem, we propose a dual-flow multiplicative update that retains the two flows separately and replaces their subtraction with a ratio of positive terms:

𝝎n,cnew∝𝝎n,c⋅1+ηn,c⋅FB+​(n,c)1+ηn,c⋅FB−​(n,c),\displaystyle\bm{\omega}^{\mathrm{new}}_{n,c}\propto\bm{\omega}_{n,c}\cdot\frac{1+\eta_{n,c}\cdot F_{\mathrm{B}}^{+}(n,c)}{1+\eta_{n,c}\cdot F_{\mathrm{B}}^{-}(n,c)}, (9)

where ηn,c:=α⋅T𝝋,𝝎​(n,c)/𝝎n,c\eta_{n,c}:=\alpha\cdot T_{\bm{\varphi},\bm{\omega}}(n,c)/\bm{\omega}_{n,c} and FB±F_{\mathrm{B}}^{\pm} denote their minibatch averages. The following proposition establishes that the update preserves valid circuit parameters, recovers standard circuit learning in the standalone setting, and agrees locally with the signed-gradient update.

Proposition 3.1 (Properties of the dual-flow update).

Fix an active sum node with normalized weights 𝛚n,c>0\bm{\omega}_{n,c}\!>\!0, flows FB±​(n,c)≥0F_{\mathrm{B}}^{\pm}(n,c)\!\geq\!0, and scales <T𝛗,𝛚​(n,c)<∞0\!<\!T_{\bm{\varphi},\bm{\omega}}(n,c)\!<\!\infty. Equation 9 satisfies:

  1. (i)

    For every α≥0\alpha\geq 0, 𝝎n,cnew>0\bm{\omega}^{\mathrm{new}}_{n,c}>0 and ∑c∈𝖼𝗁⁡(n)𝝎n,cnew=1\sum_{c\in\mathsf{ch}(n)}\bm{\omega}^{\mathrm{new}}_{n,c}=1 even when FB+​(n,c)−FB−​(n,c)<0F_{\mathrm{B}}^{+}(n,c)-F_{\mathrm{B}}^{-}(n,c)<0.

  2. (ii)

    When applied to a standalone PC with normalized inputs and sum weights, the dual-flow update in Equation 9 reduces to the standard EM update in Equation 8.

  3. (iii)

    Under (ii) and full batch B\mathrm{B}, Equation 9 recovers the full-batch EM update as α→∞\alpha\rightarrow\infty.

  4. (iv)

    As α→0\alpha\to 0, Equation 9 agrees with Equation 8 up to 𝒪⁡(α2)\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{2}).

The dual-flow update thus recovers standard circuit learning in the standalone setting and remains valid when conditional normalization introduces negative gradients. It also matches the normalized signed-gradient update to first order. Together with neural backpropagation, this enables joint training under the conditional denoising objective in Equation 7. Appendix G provides the proof.

4 Instantiating a Context-Parameterized Joint Denoiser

Having established how to jointly train the neural and circuit parameters, we now specify how the neural network uses 𝒙t\bm{x}_{t} to modulate the circuit in Equation 4. A naive parameterization would require the network to output a distinct context-dependent value for every circuit parameter, causing its output dimension to scale with the size of the circuit. Instead, we retain the shared circuit parameters 𝝎\bm{\omega} and use 𝜽t=f𝝋​(𝒙t)\bm{\theta}_{t}=f_{\bm{\varphi}}(\bm{x}_{t}) to modulate both parameterized node types: token potentials modulate the input-node distributions, while a compact set of gates reweight groups of sum-node parameters.

4.1 Learning Token Potentials

We first describe how neural token potentials modulate the circuit’s input distributions. Before modulation, each input node nn over variable XiX_{i} represents a categorical distribution πn\pi_{n} over the vocabulary 𝒱\mathcal{V}, where πn​(v)\pi_{n}(v) is the probability assigned to token vv. These probabilities belong to the circuit parameters 𝝎\bm{\omega}. Given 𝒙t\bm{x}_{t}, the neural network produces 𝜽t=f𝝋​(𝒙t)\bm{\theta}_{t}=f_{\bm{\varphi}}(\bm{x}_{t}), whose token-potential component ψt\psi_{t} assigns a nonnegative value ψt,i​(v)\psi_{t,i}(v) to each token vv for XiX_{i}. Recall that gng_{n} in Equation 6 denotes the input distribution over XiX_{i}. We obtain its modulated form by normalizing the product of the PC input distribution and the neural potentials:

gn​(v,𝜽t,𝝎)=πn​(v)​ψt,i​(v)∑v′∈𝒱πn​(v′)​ψt,i​(v′).g_{n}(v;\bm{\theta}_{t},\bm{\omega})=\frac{\pi_{n}(v)\,\psi_{t,i}(v)}{\sum_{v^{\prime}\in\mathcal{V}}\pi_{n}(v^{\prime})\,\psi_{t,i}(v^{\prime})}. (10)

Equation 10 locally normalizes the pointwise product πn​ψt,i\pi_{n}\psi_{t,i}, making gn​(⋅,𝜽t,𝝎)g_{n}(\cdot;\bm{\theta}_{t},\bm{\omega}) a categorical distribution over XiX_{i}. All input nodes over XiX_{i} share the same potential vector ψt,i\psi_{t,i}, so the neural network produces one vector per position rather than per input node. Their distinct base distributions πn\pi_{n} allow these nodes to retain different token preferences. The local normalizer depends on both the neural potentials and circuit parameters, and is retained in likelihood evaluation and differentiation.

Normalizing Equation 10 over the entire vocabulary for every input node would be computationally expensive, even though the top 1,0241{,}024 candidate tokens retain more than 99%99\% of the backbone’s predictive probability mass on average, as quantified in Figure 6 in the appendix. We therefore restrict computation to candidates favored by the backbone: at each position, we retain the top-kk logits, apply a softmax over the retained candidates, and set the remaining potentials to zero. After candidate selection, this reduces each input normalization from 𝒪⁡(|𝒱|)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{V}|) to 𝒪⁡(k)\mathcal{O}(k). During training, we ensure that the clean token is retained so that truncation does not force its likelihood to zero.

Crucially, the local normalization in Equation 10 fits directly into the dual-flow framework of Section 3. When πn\pi_{n} is learned as part of 𝝎\bm{\omega}, derivatives through both the numerator and local normalizer contribute to the positive and negative flows, respectively. The same dual-flow update can therefore optimize the input parameters together with the sum parameters. Appendix A.1 reports the choice of kk and the remaining optimization hyperparameters.

4.2 Learning Coupling Potentials

Next, we describe how neural gates can modulate the circuit’s sum weights. In practical PCs, sum parameters are typically arranged in matrices by grouping sum nodes that share the same children, and they determine how the circuit combines its child distributions (Liu et al., 2024a; Peharz et al., 2020; Loconte et al., 2025). Sum nodes sharing the same children define a row-normalized weight matrix 𝐖\mathbf{W}: rows index sum nodes and columns index child distributions. Its entries belong to 𝝎\bm{\omega}. We partition 𝐖\mathbf{W} into n×nn\times n parameter groups of width bb, each containing b×bb\times b weights. Given 𝒙t\bm{x}_{t}, a compact neural head predicts one gate per group. Exponentiating these outputs yields 𝐆t∈ℝ>0n×n\mathbf{G}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n\times n}, with each scalar gate scaling its corresponding parameter group:

𝐖t=RowNorm⁡(𝐖⊙(𝐆t⊗𝟏b×b)),\mathbf{W}_{t}=\operatorname{RowNorm}\!\left(\mathbf{W}\odot\bigl(\mathbf{G}_{t}\otimes\mathbf{1}_{b\times b}\bigr)\right), (11)

where ⊙\odot denotes elementwise multiplication, ⊗\otimes denotes the Kronecker product, 𝟏b×b\mathbf{1}_{b\times b} is an all-ones matrix, and RowNorm\operatorname{RowNorm} normalizes each row. Zero log-gates recover 𝐖\mathbf{W}, while context-dependent gates adjust the relative mixture weights. Row normalization preserves valid mixtures, and the unchanged circuit structure preserves tractable marginalization and conditioning.

Together, Equations 10 and 11 turn the PC into a context-parameterized denoiser. For each 𝒙t\bm{x}_{t}, the backbone produces both token potentials that modulate the circuit’s input distributions and group-level gates 𝐆t\mathbf{G}_{t} that reweight sum parameters. These neural outputs allow the same circuit to express context-dependent token preferences and dependencies through a compact modulation of its shared base parameters. The circuit structure remains fixed, preserving exact marginalization and conditional inference for each 𝜽t\bm{\theta}_{t}. Figure 2 compares the resulting conditional likelihoods under block diffusion. Both variants of Codpula achieve substantially lower NLL than the base model at high masking rates, with the largest improvement when the current block is fully masked.

5 Decoding from a Learned Joint Denoiser

Decoding begins from a partially masked sequence. At each denoising step tt, the learned denoiser defines a tractable joint distribution over the current set of masked variables under consideration, conditioned on the visible tokens. The decoder uses this distribution to decide what to propose and may use its joint structure to decide where to decode, i.e., which proposals to commit. Committed values become visible, while the others remain masked for subsequent steps. We first describe how proposals are obtained from the joint distribution, then review standard rules for selecting where to commit, and finally introduce our dependency-aware commitment rule.

To obtain proposals, we use the current neural outputs 𝜽t\bm{\theta}_{t} to modulate the circuit’s input distributions and sum weights as in Equations 10 and 11. Before sampling, we control the sharpness of the neural token preferences by dividing the backbone logits by a temperature γ>0\gamma>0 before normalization. Writing ψt,i\psi_{t,i} for the unscaled token potentials, the resulting input distribution is

gn(γ)​(v,𝜽t,𝝎)=πn​(v)​ψt,i​(v)1/γ∑v′∈𝒱πn​(v′)​ψt,i​(v′)1/γ.\displaystyle g_{n}^{(\gamma)}(v;\bm{\theta}_{t},\bm{\omega})=\frac{\pi_{n}(v)\,\psi_{t,i}(v)^{1/\gamma}}{\sum_{v^{\prime}\in\mathcal{V}}\pi_{n}(v^{\prime})\,\psi_{t,i}(v^{\prime})^{1/\gamma}}.

Temperature scaling thus acts on the neural potentials within each input distribution, retaining the learned categorical parameters πn\pi_{n} and the current modulated sum weights. We then condition the circuit on the visible tokens and jointly sample the masked variables under consideration.

Once token proposals have been sampled, the decoder decides which positions to commit. The joint denoiser supports standard confidence-, margin-, and entropy-based selection, as well as random selection (Nie et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2025). Our dependency-aware decoder retains these rules for candidate selection, then uses the joint distribution to assess dependencies among the candidates before commitment. Beyond these tokenwise criteria, the learned joint distribution provides conditional queries for adapting which proposals are committed together.

We first form proposals for all masked tokens under consideration (e.g., those in the current block for block diffusion). For each such token ii, let 𝒙^−i\hat{\bm{x}}^{-i} denote the proposals at all other positions under consideration. We measure how conditioning on them changes the log-probability of x^i\hat{x}^{i}:

δi=|log⁡p𝝋,𝝎​(x^i∣𝒙^−i,𝒙t)−log⁡p𝝋,𝝎​(x^i∣𝒙t)|.\delta_{i}=\left|\log p_{\bm{\varphi},\bm{\omega}}\!\left(\hat{x}^{i}\mid\hat{\bm{x}}^{-i},\bm{x}_{t}\right)-\log p_{\bm{\varphi},\bm{\omega}}\!\left(\hat{x}^{i}\mid\bm{x}_{t}\right)\right|. (12)

Here, δi\delta_{i} is the absolute conditional pointwise mutual information between proposal ii and the rest, where smaller values indicate weaker dependence. We commit tokens with δi<τ\delta_{i}<\tau (τ>0\tau>0) and defer the rest, committing the lowest-scoring token if none qualify. Deferred tokens are reconsidered at the next step under the updated context. For mm tokens, all scores require one complete-assignment, mm singleton, and mm leave-one-out marginals. These queries share the visible-evidence normalizer, can be batched with the same neural outputs, and require no additional backbone evaluations. Algorithm 3 gives the block-decoding instantiation; Appendix D.1 details the queries and overhead.

6 Experiments

We evaluate Codpula on mathematical reasoning and code generation using four modern dLLM backbones. We examine its accuracy across parallel-decoding budgets, its accuracy–latency trade-off under adaptive commitment, and the contributions of input and coupling modulation.

Models and training. Our experiments include LLaDA-1.0-8B-Instruct (Nie et al., 2025), LLaDA-2.0-mini (Bie et al., 2025), Dream-v0-Instruct-7B (Ye et al., 2025), and SDAR-8B-Chat-b16 (Cheng et al., 2025). For LLaDA models, we use two-stage training: we first train the PC with the backbone frozen, then update the backbone through LoRA adapters while keeping the PC fixed. For Dream and SDAR, we jointly optimize the PC and the backbone adapters. The two-stage schedule for LLaDA is motivated by the sensitivity to finetuning among this family.

Baselines. We use static decoding with the original instruction-tuned backbone as our reference and compare against both training-based and training-free baselines. CE-SFT trains LoRA adapters with masked token cross-entropy, whereas CoDD (Li et al., 2026) couples the frozen backbone’s predictions with a separately trained PC. The training-free baselines include Dynamic Conf. (Wu et al., 2025), DUS (Luxembourg et al., 2026), ReMDM (Wang et al., 2025), and Tolerator (Tian et al., 2025), all of which modify only the decoding procedure while keeping the backbone frozen. Appendix A provides supporting evidence for the LLaDA training schedule, full training and decoding configurations, and detailed descriptions of the decoding baselines.

Mathematical reasoning. We evaluate LLaDA-1.0, LLaDA-2.0, and Dream on MATH500 (Lightman et al., 2023) and GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), using all 500 and 1,319 test problems, respectively. For LLaDA-2.0, we additionally evaluate on AIME 2024 and AIME 2025 (Art of Problem Solving, ), using combined AIME I and II in each year with chain-of-thought prompting. All mathematical reasoning evaluations are zero-shot and use the lm-evaluation-harness framework (Gao et al., 2024). We report final-answer accuracy, using mathematical equivalence checking for MATH500 and exact match after answer extraction for GSM8K. For AIME, we prioritize the final boxed answer during extraction and report exact-match accuracy after string normalization.

Code generation. For code generation, LLaDA-1.0 and Dream are evaluated on MBPP (Austin et al., 2021b) and HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), while SDAR is evaluated on the extended-test variants, MBPP+ and HumanEval+ (Liu et al., 2023). The extended test suites provide a more stringent assessment of the functional correctness of generated programs. All code-generation evaluations use zero-shot instruction-style prompts, with performance measured by pass@1. Dataset sizes are summarized in Appendix 7, with evaluation details provided in the same appendix.

Training through the joint model improves parallel prediction. On LLaDA-2.0 GSM8K (Table 1), CE-SFT nearly matches Codpula at two tokens per step but falls below the backbone at eight. Codpula improves over the backbone in both settings, by 11.111.1 and 21.221.2 percentage points, respectively. Thus, improvements from tokenwise fine-tuning do not necessarily translate to effective parallel prediction. The ablation in Table 16 supports training through the circuit: backbone adaptation adds gains over fitted circuit in seven of ten settings.

Context-dependent coupling provides additional, task-dependent gains. Input-only Codpula already improves over the backbone across multiple settings (Tables 1 and 3). Sum modulation provides further gains, most clearly on Dream’s full-sequence HumanEval+ evaluation (Table 2): it improves the input-only variant at one to four tokens per step, including a setting where that variant falls below the backbone. These results indicate that adapting mixture weights can improve on token reweighting alone, with benefits that depend on the task and decoding regime.

The gains extend to measured generation latency. Figures 3 and 4 show improved accuracy–latency trade-offs after accounting for circuit computation, with adaptive decoding improving selected operating points. This improvement comes despite additional computation: on LLaDA-1.0/MATH500, adaptive Codpula incurs 6.86.8–8.2%8.2\% overhead at matched numbers of backbone evaluations (Table 12). Under EOS-based stopping, latency also reflects generation length; the shorter generations in Table 11 therefore contribute to the observed speedups (Appendix A.3.2).

7 Related Work and Conclusion

Joint prediction and adaptive decoding.

Masked diffusion models, including MDLM and MD4 (Sahoo et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024), LLaDA and Dream (Nie et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025), and block-diffusion models (Arriola et al., 2025), typically factorize predictions across positions, omitting dependencies among parallel outputs. Remedies include auxiliary copulas (Liu et al., 2025a), sequence-level energy corrections (Xu et al., 2025a), and mixture-based distillation (Hayakawa et al., 2025). CoDD couples a frozen denoiser with a learned circuit prior (Li et al., 2026), while tensor-train modeling predicts context-conditioned joint distributions through a modified output head (Kim and Sung, 2026). Complementary decoding strategies improve token ordering (Kim et al., 2025), adapt parallelism using confidence or entropy (Wu et al., 2025; Ben-Hamu et al., 2025), assess parallel proposals with an auxiliary autoregressive model (Israel et al., 2025), or remask generated tokens (Wang et al., 2025). We jointly learn token potentials and context-dependent coupling under a conditional objective and query the resulting joint distribution for adaptive commitment.

Probabilistic circuits and their applications.

Probabilistic circuits represent expressive joint distributions with tractable marginalization and conditioning (Poon and Domingos, 2011; Choi et al., 2020). Neural extensions use network outputs to parameterize context-dependent distributions (Shao et al., 2020; Yidou-Weng et al., 2026; Grivas et al., 2026). PCs and related models also guide constrained autoregressive generation (Zhang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024) and diffusion-based image inpainting (Liu et al., 2024b). We integrate the circuit into the denoiser, modulate its coupling parameters with backbone outputs, and train the neural components through it. Building on Anemone’s minibatch EM update (Liu et al., 2025b), we develop a multiplicative update that accommodates signed flows from conditional normalization while preserving valid circuit parameters.

In this work, we introduce Codpula, a context-parameterized joint denoiser that learns token predictions and their coupling while retaining exact normalization and conditional inference. To support conditional training, we derive a dual-flow update, and the learned joint distribution enables dependence-adaptive decoding. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation show improved accuracy-latency trade-offs across multiple backbones. Additional circuit computation and fixed-size coupling windows remain as limitations, motivating more efficient inference and joint modeling over longer sequences.

Appendix A Experiment Details

A.1 Training

SFT on LLaDA.

Continued fine-tuning does not consistently improve instruction-tuned LLaDA models, especially on mathematical ability. In d1, supervised fine-tuning improves over LLaDA-8B-Instruct in only seven of twelve evaluated settings (Zhao et al., 2025). On LLaDA-1.5, DSFT reports that standard SFT offers negligible or even negative effects on the downstream tasks (Chen and Chen, 2025). Similarly, Sun et al. (2025) report a decrease on MATH from 31.7%31.7\% to 29.6%29.6\% under classical SFT. CDLM provides a similar observation: its initial LLaDA-1.0 training on approximately 7500 Bespoke prompts reduces GSM8K accuracy from 77.1%77.1\% to 72.1%72.1\% (Kim et al., 2026). Taken together, these findings motivate treating the backbone update schedule as a consequential design choice. We therefore separate circuit training from backbone fitting for LLaDA model family and retain an independently tuned CE-SFT baseline in the comparison.

Training data and masking.

For each sequence, we sample a masking probability tt uniformly from [0,1)[0,1) and independently mask response tokens with probability tt. Prompt tokens remain visible, and padding positions are excluded from the supervised region. The backbone processes the resulting masked sequence; its predictions over the response are then divided into 32-token blocks for circuit training. When the response length is not divisible by 32, we add a final, right-aligned block covering the last 32 response tokens. This block overlaps the preceding block and preserves the response ending without introducing additional padding targets. Responses shorter than a complete block are excluded from circuit training.

  • •

    Mathematical Reasoning. For LLaDA-1.0, both training stages use the same subset of 1,910 hard problems from NuminaMath (LI et al., 2024), selected according to the frozen backbone’s denoising loss. LLaDA-2.0 uses the full NuminaMath dataset in both stages, while Dream uses the same full dataset during joint training.

  • •

    Code Generation. All models use the same training mixture constructed from JinaAI Code Exercises (Jina AI, 2023), KodCode-V1 (Xu et al., 2025b), CodeFeedback-Filtered-Instruction (Zheng et al., 2024), and the non-test splits of MBPP (Austin et al., 2021b). The mixture contains 98,660 examples in HumanEval- and MBPP-style formats and is used in both training stages for LLaDA-1.0 and during joint training for Dream and SDAR.

PC configurations.

We use homogeneous hidden Markov models with 1,0241{,}024 latent states per position, compiled into probabilistic circuits. The circuit sequence length is 32 for LLaDA-1.0, LLaDA-2.0, and Dream, and 16 for SDAR. Transition parameters are shared across positions, and categorical leaf distributions are parameterized over the full vocabulary of the corresponding backbone. We train separate circuits for each backbone and task family. Within each backbone and task family, CoDD and Codpula use the same circuit architecture. Parameter conditioning modulates the circuit’s sum weights while preserving its topology. Training hyperparameters are summarized in Table 5. Circuit training retains the backbone’s top-1,0241{,}024 evidence candidates per position; an ablation on LLaDA-1.0 examines this choice and its compatibility with full-vocabulary decoding in Section B.2.

Shared training settings.

All Codpula runs use Anemone EM with momentum 0.9 and evidence temperature 1.0. Adapters are optimized with AdamW without bias adaptation, rsLoRA, or an auxiliary cross-entropy loss. Each GPU processes two sequences per microbatch; padding positions are unsupervised, and gradients on observed evidence are masked. Among the configurations in Table 5, only LLaDA2.0 uses gradient clipping, with a maximum norm of 1.0. Parameter conditioning is enabled in Codpula (Both) by training the router at a learning rate of 10−310^{-3} for SDAR and for both Dream task families. For SDAR, Codpula (Input Only) keeps the router fixed at its uniform initialization with learning rate zero; all other hyperparameters are identical to those of Codpula (Both). Module group A adapts per-block query, key, value, and feed-forward output projections, together with the vocabulary head and token embeddings; B adapts fused QKV and the shared-expert MLP; C adapts all attention and MLP projections; and D adapts only query, key, and value projections.

Baseline training and hyperparameter selection.

CE-SFT trains an independent LoRA adapter with the masked-token cross-entropy objective, while CoDD trains a circuit with the backbone frozen. We tune the baselines independently for each backbone and task family. For CE-SFT, the search covers the adapter learning rate, effective batch size, LoRA rank rr, scaling ratio α/r\alpha/r, and number of training updates. For CoDD, we vary the EM step size, response-block accumulation threshold, and training duration. Intermediate checkpoints are evaluated by downstream generation accuracy, and we report the best-performing configuration for each baseline. The selected baseline configurations are summarized in Table 6; their learning rates, batch sizes, and LoRA settings are selected independently of Codpula’s. Sequence batch size and response-block accumulation are distinct quantities and are reported in their respective units.

A.2 Evaluation

A.3 Decoding

A.3.1 Decoding rules chosen for the base

For the fixed-schedule comparisons among Base, CE-SFT, CoDD, and Codpula, we use the same token-selection rule for each backbone–benchmark pair. LLaDA-1.0 uses low-confidence decoding on GSM8K, MATH500, and HumanEval, and margin decoding on MBPP. Dream uses low-confidence decoding on the math benchmarks and entropy decoding on the coding benchmarks. LLaDA-2.0 and SDAR use low-confidence decoding. Each rule is held fixed across methods and tokens-per-step settings within the corresponding comparison.

Table 9 reports additional LLaDA-1.0 results under alternative token-selection rules. Their relative performance varies with the benchmark and degree of parallelism. On GSM8K, Codpula improves over the base model at every evaluated tokens-per-step setting under random decoding. Under margin decoding on the same benchmark, it performs similarly to the base model at 2, 4, and 8 tokens per step, while improving accuracy from 10.1%10.1\% to 15.7%15.7\% at 16 tokens per step and from 1.7%1.7\% to 5.6%5.6\% at 32 tokens per step. Thus, its gains at high parallelism also extend to alternative token-selection rules.

Table 10 additionally reports Dream coding results under block diffusion with low-confidence decoding and a maximum generation length of 512 tokens. Both Codpula variants outperform the base model in every reported setting. At four tokens per step, Codpula improves HumanEval accuracy from 28.7%28.7\% to 39.6%39.6\%, while Codpula (Both) improves MBPP accuracy from 40.1%40.1\% to 51.4%51.4\%. These results show that Codpula’s coding gains also extend to low-confidence decoding.

A.3.2 Early Stopping Effects

We enable EOS-based early stopping for LLaDA-2.0 on AIME and for SDAR on the coding benchmarks. Consequently, fixing the number of tokens decoded per step does not fix the total number of generated tokens or denoising steps: these also depend on when each generation terminates. Table 11 reports mean generation lengths and end-to-end runtimes for LLaDA-2.0-mini and Codpula on AIME24 and AIME25. At each matched tokens-per-step setting, Codpula produces shorter generations and has lower latency. For example, as shown in table 11, on AIME24 at four tokens per step, the mean generation length decreases from 7,870.7 to 4,080.8 tokens, and the mean runtime decreases from 411.2 to 163.9 seconds per question. These latency differences reflect both the cost per denoising step and the amount of generation performed.

Early stopping also explains the nonmonotonic runtime of the SDAR curves in Figure 4. More aggressive parallel decoding can delay EOS prediction, increasing the number of generated blocks enough to offset the reduction in denoising steps per block. For example, the SDAR base model on HumanEval+ executes an average of 31.53 forward passes per question at four tokens per step, compared with 36.09 at eight and 37.45 at sixteen. Thus, increasing parallelism can reduce accuracy while increasing runtime. To separate per-block denoising effort from variation in generation length, Figure 5 plots accuracy against the mean number of denoising steps per block. This complements the wall-clock comparison by showing decoding quality at comparable per-block step counts.

A.3.3 Post-hoc Baseline methods

Dynamic conf.

Dynamic confidence-threshold decoding (Wu et al., 2025) adaptively determines the number of tokens unmasked at each decoding step. It accepts predictions at masked positions whose confidence exceeds a fixed threshold, leaving the remaining positions masked for subsequent steps. If no prediction exceeds the threshold, the highest-confidence prediction is accepted to ensure progress. Unlike static decoding, which follows a predetermined token-unmasking schedule, Dynamic Conf. allows more tokens to be decoded in parallel when the model is confident, without updating the backbone parameters.

DUS.

The Dilated Unmasking Scheduler (DUS) (Luxembourg et al., 2026) accelerates masked-diffusion decoding by replacing confidence based token selection with a deterministic, coarse-to-fine schedule. At each denoising step, it reveals a group of positions that are distributed approximately uniformly across the remaining masked sequence; subsequent steps progressively reduce the spacing until the block is complete. By spacing simultaneously decoded tokens apart, dilation reduces their mutual dependence without requiring confidence based ranking. We therefore use the paper’s main dilated schedule as the DUS baseline and vary its number of passes per block to compare it with our method at matched computation budgets. With 32 token blocks, the standard DUS schedule supports at most five forward passes. We report the two and four pass settings that match our decoder budgets. Additionally, we disable confidence based remasking because rejected tokens are not regenerated by the fixed schedule, leaving permanent mask holes. For larger budgets in the wall-clock curves, we report DUS (ext.), which subdivides the final reveal group into consecutive smaller passes while preserving the original position order. For example, a final group of eight positions can be executed as 4+44+4 or 2+2+2+22+2+2+2, with the model reevaluated after each subgroup so later predictions condition on earlier commitments. This extension leaves the preceding dilation schedule unchanged.

ReMDM.

The remasking diffusion model (ReMDM) sampler (Wang et al., 2025) augments the reverse diffusion process with self correction: instead of treating every revealed token as permanent, it may remask previously generated tokens and predict them again using the improved surrounding context available at a later denoising step. A time dependent remasking probability σt\sigma_{t} controls how aggressively the decoder revises its current solution. The paper studies several schedules for this probability, including capped, rescaled, confidence weighted, switch, and loop based schedules; the switch formulation delays remasking until a chosen stage so that early steps can first construct a coherent draft. We use the switch-style formulation on top of LLaDA’s low-confidence decoder because it preserves the original decoding budget while allowing uncertain decisions to be revised.

Tolerator.

Finish First, Perfect Later (Tolerator) separates generation into a filling stage and a refinement stage (Tian et al., 2025). The fill up stage first produces a complete draft using the standard diffusion decoding process, with an end-of-text penalty to discourage premature termination. During refinement, a random subset of non-prompt tokens is remasked and regenerated while the remaining draft tokens serve as context for validating these predictions. The remasking rate is gradually reduced with a cosine schedule, enabling broad corrections early in refinement and more stable, localized revisions later. The paper allocates half of the forward-pass budget to each stage. We use this fill and refine strategy as a training-free baseline at matched computation budgets. We use per block refinement because LLaDA2.0’s block causal attention is trained with completed preceding blocks; refining each block before proceeding preserves this structure, whereas full draft refinement introduces masks into earlier context.

A.3.4 Wall-Clock Time Measurement

All timing measurements use a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU with no competing process and a sequence batch size of 1, corresponding to serving one request at a time. GPU isolation is verified before and after each measurement. LoRA adapters are merged into the backbone before timing, and we report median timings over repeated measurements after warm-up. Timing excludes model loading, tokenization, detokenization, evaluation-harness overhead, and grading.

Table 12 reports Codpula’s additional cost per backbone function evaluation (NFE), measured using the same protocol under uniform and adaptive decoding, with and without parameter conditioning. Measurements use fixed input shapes; adaptive overhead additionally includes a dependence-deferral query at the specified width. Parameter conditioning includes both router evaluation and conditioned circuit computation.

A.4 Computational Resources

All experiments, including training and inference, are conducted on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs. We observed hardware-dependent differences in experimental results and therefore use the same GPU model throughout to maintain consistent comparisons.

Appendix B Ablation Studies

B.1 Decoding Configurations

Dream with full-sequence diffusion.

We also evaluate Dream under full-sequence diffusion with entropy decoding and a generation length of 128 tokens. Table 13 shows that both Codpula variants outperform the base model in every reported setting. At four tokens per step, HumanEval accuracy increases from 26.8%26.8\% for the base model to 32.9%32.9\% for Codpula and 41.5%41.5\% for Codpula (Both). Parameter conditioning improves several settings, although Codpula without parameter conditioning achieves higher accuracy on all three benchmarks at eight tokens per step. These results demonstrate that Codpula is also effective under full-sequence diffusion.

SDAR with block size 32.

We additionally evaluate SDAR-8B-Chat-b32 with a matching 32-token circuit, extending the block-size-16 setting used in the main text. Table 14 shows that Codpula improves over the base model at every evaluated setting on MBPP+. On HumanEval+, it improves accuracy at 4–32 tokens per step, matches the base model at two tokens per step, and underperforms at one token per step. At four tokens per step, accuracy increases from 15.9% to 35.2% on MBPP+ and from 31.7% to 40.9% on HumanEval+. These results show that the benefits of coupling extend to a larger decoding block, particularly when several tokens are committed simultaneously.

B.2 Evidence Truncation

We examine the effect of restricting circuit evidence to the backbone’s top-1,0241{,}024 candidates per position on LLaDA-1.0. During training, we retain these entries from the backbone’s log-probability vector, whereas decoding uses the full vocabulary of 126,464126{,}464 tokens by default. This truncation restricts the supplied evidence; the circuit’s categorical leaves remain parameterized over the full vocabulary.

For backbone logits ℓ\bm{\ell} and evidence temperature τ\tau, we measure the discarded probability mass as

mk​(ℓ,τ)=1−∑v∈Sk​(ℓ)softmax⁡(ℓ/τ)v,k=1,024,m_{k}(\bm{\ell},\tau)=1-\sum_{v\in S_{k}(\bm{\ell})}\operatorname{softmax}(\bm{\ell}/\tau)_{v},\qquad k=1{,}024, (13)

where Sk​(ℓ)S_{k}(\bm{\ell}) contains the kk highest-scoring tokens. Figure 6 reports measurements over 46,08046{,}080 positions. At the training temperature τ=1\tau=1, the mean discarded mass is 0.53%0.53\%, with 19.6%19.6\% of positions exceeding 1%1\% and a maximum of 13.2%13.2\%. At the evaluated decoding temperatures τ∈{0.05,0.1,0.2,0.3}\tau\in\{0.05,0.1,0.2,0.3\}, the measured mean residual is numerically negligible, on the order of 10−810^{-8}. Temperature sharpening therefore concentrates nearly all backbone probability mass within the retained candidate set.

We separately ablate truncation during training and decoding on GSM8K with 200 evaluation examples, a maximum generation length of 256, and block length 32. Table 15 supports truncating evidence during training, while showing no observed accuracy loss from applying the same truncation at decoding. We use full-vocabulary evidence by default at inference, but top-1,0241{,}024 evidence is an empirically equivalent alternative in these comparisons.

B.3 Contributions of Individual Components

Confidence for token commitment.

Codpula’s refined distributions determine token proposals and can also guide the choice of positions to commit. We ablate this second role on SDAR by comparing confidence scores from the backbone with those from Codpula. Both variants use Codpula’s token proposals and the same dependence-based deferral rule; the confidence source determines the ranking of candidate positions. As shown in Figure 7, Codpula confidence generally improves the accuracy–runtime trade-off at moderate and larger budgets for both Input Only and Both, while backbone confidence remains competitive at the smallest budgets. Thus, the refined distributions provide useful information for the commitment schedule as well as for token prediction.

Stage-1 circuit and backbone adaptation.

Table 16 separates the contributions of the stage-1 circuit and the stage-2 backbone adapter on LLaDA-1.0. The stage-1 circuit alone improves over the base model at every reported setting. Adding the stage-2 adapter yields further gains in seven of ten settings, including 4.7 percentage points on MBPP at both two and four tokens per step and 3.1 points on HumanEval at eight tokens per step. The complete model also matches or exceeds CE-SFT at every setting. Differences between the stage-1 and CoDD circuits vary in sign, ranging from −2.0-2.0 to +3.5+3.5 points. All baselines are independently tuned over learning rates and training budgets, and we report the best-performing configuration for each. The additional gains from stage-2 adaptation, with the stage-1 circuit held fixed, demonstrate the contribution of training the backbone through the circuit.

B.4 Circuit Removal at Inference

Removing the PC at inference is not an appropriate way to isolate its contribution. The adapted backbone and PC together define Codpula’s normalized conditional distribution, and the adapter is trained under this complete distribution’s conditional-likelihood objective. The backbone outputs serve as token potentials within the circuit and are not optimized as standalone denoising probabilities. Removing the PC and decoding directly from these potentials therefore substitutes a different distribution for the trained model. We consequently do not report circuit-removal results as a component ablation. Backbone adaptation without a circuit is instead evaluated using the independently trained CE-SFT baseline.

B.5 Evidence-Temperature Sensitivity

We vary the evidence temperature τ\tau while holding the LLaDA-1.0 backbone adapter, circuit, and decoding rule fixed. Table 17 shows that the preferred temperature depends on the decoding budget. Among the temperatures shown, the best value shifts from τ=0.05\tau=0.05 at 256 steps to τ=0.5\tau=0.5 at 32 steps, with τ=0.1\tau=0.1 preferred at the intermediate budgets. A finer sweep at 32 steps gives 11.2%11.2\%, 11.6%11.6\%, and 11.2%11.2\% accuracy at τ=0.5\tau=0.5, 0.60.6, and 0.70.7, respectively. These results motivate selecting the evidence temperature separately for each decoding budget.

B.6 Additional Results

B.6.1 AIME Benchmarks

We provide additional accuracy–time comparisons on AIME24 and AIME25 using LLaDA-2.0-mini. On AIME25, adaptive Codpula matches the base model’s 10%10\% accuracy with a 3.84×3.84\times speedup (Figure 8). Figure 9 shows results across decoding configurations on both benchmarks. On AIME24, uniform Codpula reaches 53.3%53.3\% accuracy, while adaptive Codpula matches the base model’s 40%40\% accuracy at a lower time cost. On AIME25, the gains are concentrated in the lower-latency region; several baselines attain higher accuracy at larger time budgets.

D.1 Dependence Queries and Decoding Cost

We evaluate Equation 12 using marginal queries to a single circuit instantiated from the current neural outputs 𝜽t=f𝝋​(𝒙t)\bm{\theta}_{t}=f_{\bm{\varphi}}(\bm{x}_{t}). The neural token potentials, coupling gates, and local normalizers remain fixed across these queries; only the observed assignments change. All probabilities below refer to the circuit used for dependence scoring, with its evidence temperature and vocabulary support held fixed.

log⁡p𝝋,𝝎​(x^i∣^​𝒙𝒞∖{i},𝒙t)\displaystyle\log p_{\bm{\varphi},\bm{\omega}}(\hat{x}^{i}\mid\hat{}\bm{x}^{\mathcal{C}\setminus\{i\}},\bm{x}_{t}) =ℓ⁡(𝒞)−ℓ⁡(𝒞∖{i}).\displaystyle=\ell(\mathcal{C})-\ell(\mathcal{C}\setminus\{i\}).

Thus, for m=|𝒞|m=|\mathcal{C}|, the scores use one complete-candidate marginal, mm singleton marginals, and mm leave-one-out marginals. Computing these 2​m+12m+1 probabilities requires at most 2​m+22m+2 circuit evaluations, including the shared normalizer. A cached normalizer can be reused only when it was computed with the same circuit parameters, neural evidence, and visible assignments. Duplicate queries can also be reused; for m=1m=1, the score is zero without any additional query.

Batched circuit evaluation.

We batch the evidence assignments e∅e_{\varnothing}, e𝒞e_{\mathcal{C}}, {e{i}:i∈𝒞}\{e_{\{i\}}:i\in\mathcal{C}\}, and {e𝒞∖{i}:i∈𝒞}\{e_{\mathcal{C}\setminus\{i\}}:i\in\mathcal{C}\} in one circuit call. Each batch item uses the same modulated circuit and differs only in which variables are observed. At an input node, an observed variable contributes its probability under the modulated input distribution, while an unobserved variable contributes the local normalizer log⁡Zn,i\log Z_{n,i}. The bottom-up computation in Appendix F.1 then returns ℓ⁡(S)\ell(S) for each evidence assignment, marginalizing over all unresolved tokens and circuit latent variables. The input normalizers can be shared across the batch. After input preparation, the total circuit work is O⁡(m​|E|)O(m|E|) for m≥2m\geq 2, where |E||E| is the number of circuit edges. Batching parallelizes these evaluations and requires no additional Transformer evaluation.

Computation and measured overhead.

Dependence evaluation adds circuit computation but reuses the current neural outputs, requiring no additional backbone evaluation within a step. Figures 1 and 2 report the resulting accuracy–latency trade-offs under adaptive decoding. Table 12 quantifies the additional cost relative to backbone-only decoding at matched NFE, while Appendix A.3.4 describes the measurement protocol.

Appendix E Derivation of the Joint Denoising Objective

We derive Equation 7 as a lower-bound training objective obtained from the diffusion ELBO. Consider sequences of fixed length LL under independent absorbing masking, where αt\alpha_{t} denotes the masking probability. Assume a differentiable increasing schedule with α0=0\alpha_{0}=0 and α1=1\alpha_{1}=1. The joint denoiser p𝝋,𝝎​(𝒙0∣𝒙t)p_{\bm{\varphi},\bm{\omega}}(\bm{x}_{0}\mid\bm{x}_{t}) assigns probability only to clean completions consistent with the visible tokens.

The continuous-time reverse process reveals each masked position at rate α˙t/αt\dot{\alpha}_{t}/\alpha_{t}, using the corresponding token marginal of the joint denoiser. Writing ℳt\mathcal{M}_{t} for the masked positions, the standard diffusion ELBO takes the form  (Sahoo et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024)

ℰ⁡(𝝎,𝝋)=∫01α˙tαt​𝔼𝒙0,𝒙t​[∑i∈ℳtlog⁡p𝝋,𝝎​(x0i∣𝒙t)]​𝑑t,\mathcal{E}(\bm{\omega},\bm{\varphi})=\int_{0}^{1}\frac{\dot{\alpha}_{t}}{\alpha_{t}}\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x}_{0},\bm{x}_{t}}\!\left[\sum_{i\in\mathcal{M}_{t}}\log p_{\bm{\varphi},\bm{\omega}}(x_{0}^{i}\mid\bm{x}_{t})\right]\,\mathrm{d}t, (17)

We assume the usual integrability and endpoint conditions for the continuous-time bound.

To relate this expression to the conditional joint likelihood, observe that each token marginal sums over completions that include 𝒙0\bm{x}_{0}. Consequently,

p𝝋,𝝎​(x0i∣𝒙t)≥p𝝋,𝝎​(𝒙0∣𝒙t).p_{\bm{\varphi},\bm{\omega}}(x_{0}^{i}\mid\bm{x}_{t})\geq p_{\bm{\varphi},\bm{\omega}}(\bm{x}_{0}\mid\bm{x}_{t}). (18)

Appendix F Additional Details on Probabilistic Circuits

F.1 Structure and Exact Inference

We state the structural properties that guarantee tractable computation of ZZ. Let ϕ⁡(n){\phi}(n) denote the variables appearing in the input nodes descending from node nn.

Definition F.1 (Smoothness).

A PC is smooth if all children of every sum node nn have the same scope:

ϕ⁡(c)=ϕ⁡(n),∀c∈𝖼𝗁⁡(n).{\phi}(c)={\phi}(n),\qquad\forall c\in\mathsf{ch}(n).
Definition F.2 (Decomposability).

A PC is decomposable if the children of every product node nn have pairwise disjoint scopes:

ϕ⁡(c)∩ϕ⁡(d)=∅,∀c,d∈𝖼𝗁⁡(n),c≠d.{\phi}(c)\cap{\phi}(d)=\varnothing,\qquad\forall c,d\in\mathsf{ch}(n),\ c\neq d.
Bottom-up evaluation.

Given observed token assignments ee, let Ln​(e)L_{n}(e) denote the probability of the evidence within ϕ⁡(n){\phi}(n). At an input node, we evaluate the observed token’s probability or sum over all token values if the variable is unobserved. Product nodes combine evidence from disjoint scopes by multiplication, while sum nodes average their children’s evidence probabilities using the mixture weights:

Ln​(e)={gn​(ei),n​ is an input over observed ​Xi,∑v∈𝒱gn​(v)=1,n​ is an input over unobserved ​Xi,∏c∈𝖼𝗁⁡(n)Lc​(e),n​ is a product node,∑c∈𝖼𝗁⁡(n)ωn,c​Lc​(e),n​ is a sum node.L_{n}(e)=\begin{cases}g_{n}(e_{i}),&n\text{ is an input over observed }X_{i},\\ \sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}g_{n}(v)=1,&n\text{ is an input over unobserved }X_{i},\\ \prod_{c\in\mathsf{ch}(n)}L_{c}(e),&n\text{ is a product node},\\ \sum_{c\in\mathsf{ch}(n)}\omega_{n,c}L_{c}(e),&n\text{ is a sum node}.\end{cases}

Smoothness and decomposability ensure that these local operations compute the exact evidence probability. Evaluating each node after its children yields this probability at the root in a single pass, with cost linear in the number of circuit edges after input evaluation.

Mapping the modulated circuit to tractable inference.

Appendix D of Li et al. (2026) establishes tractable normalization by expressing its normalizer as an independent soft-evidence query on a PC. We follow the same reasoning, accounting for modulation of both input distributions and sum weights.

Fix the masked context 𝒙t\bm{x}_{t} and neural outputs 𝜽t=f𝝋​(𝒙t)\bm{\theta}_{t}=f_{\bm{\varphi}}(\bm{x}_{t}). The input modulation in Equation 10 preserves each input node’s univariate scope and produces a normalized distribution. Likewise, the gates in Equation 11 produce nonnegative, normalized sum weights without changing the children of any node. Assuming positive local normalizers, the resulting p~​(𝒙0,𝜽t,𝝎)\tilde{p}(\bm{x}_{0};\bm{\theta}_{t},\bm{\omega}) is therefore a normalized PC with the same smoothness and decomposability properties as the original circuit. Although the neural outputs depend on the full context, they remain fixed as we sum over 𝒙0\bm{x}_{0}.

The normalizer in Equation 5 can consequently be written as

Z(𝜽t,𝝎)=∑𝒙0p~(𝒙0;𝜽t,𝝎)∏i:xti≠[MASK]𝟏{x0i=xti}.Z(\bm{\theta}_{t},\bm{\omega})=\sum_{\bm{x}_{0}}\tilde{p}(\bm{x}_{0};\bm{\theta}_{t},\bm{\omega})\prod_{i:\,x_{t}^{i}\neq\texttt{[MASK]}}\mathbf{1}\{x_{0}^{i}=x_{t}^{i}\}. (22)

The indicators are univariate evidence functions, so Equation 22 is an independent-evidence query on the modulated PC. The tractable inference result of Liu et al. (2024b, Theorem 1) therefore applies.

Concretely, each observed input is evaluated at its visible token, while each masked input sums to one. These values propagate through the product nodes and the sum nodes using their gated weights, yielding ZZ at the root. Once the modulated parameters and input values have been computed, this bottom-up pass is exact and linear in the number of circuit edges.

F.2 Correspondence with Standard Circuit Learning Algorithms

We make explicit how Equation 8 recovers the basic updates of full-batch EM, interpolated mini-batch EM, and Anemone. Consider a standalone smooth, decomposable PC with normalized inputs and strictly positive, normalized sum weights. For a batch B\mathrm{B}, define

FB+​(n,c):=1|B|​∑𝒙∈B∂log⁡p~​(𝒙,𝝎)∂log⁡𝝎n,c,CB​(n):=∑c∈𝖼𝗁⁡(n)FB+​(n,c).F_{\mathrm{B}}^{+}(n,c):=\frac{1}{|\mathrm{B}|}\sum_{\bm{x}\in\mathrm{B}}\frac{\partial\log\tilde{p}(\bm{x};\bm{\omega})}{\partial\log\bm{\omega}_{n,c}},\qquad C_{\mathrm{B}}(n):=\sum_{c\in\mathsf{ch}(n)}F_{\mathrm{B}}^{+}(n,c). (23)

The inputs are held fixed, and derivatives treat untied edge weights as independent coordinates before row normalization. These derivatives are posterior expected edge counts (Peharz et al., 2020); CB​(n)C_{\mathrm{B}}(n) is their total for node nn. Here p~\tilde{p} denotes the raw circuit output, which equals the model likelihood at normalized parameters. The derivatives do not include an additional global normalizer or a softmax parameterization.

Writing Tn,c:=T𝝋,𝝎​(n,c)T_{n,c}:=T_{\bm{\varphi},\bm{\omega}}(n,c), the row-normalized form of Equation 8 in this standalone setting is

𝝎n,cnew=𝝎n,c+α​Tn,c​FB+​(n,c)1+α​∑d∈𝖼𝗁⁡(n)Tn,d​FB+​(n,d).\bm{\omega}^{\mathrm{new}}_{n,c}=\frac{\bm{\omega}_{n,c}+\alpha T_{n,c}F_{\mathrm{B}}^{+}(n,c)}{1+\alpha\sum_{d\in\mathsf{ch}(n)}T_{n,d}F_{\mathrm{B}}^{+}(n,d)}. (24)

All quantities on the right are evaluated before the update. The following choices establish the correspondence.

Full-batch EM.

Let B=𝒟\mathrm{B}=\mathcal{D} be the full training set and take Tn,c=1T_{n,c}=1. If C𝒟​(n)>0C_{\mathcal{D}}(n)>0, then

limα→∞𝝎n,cnew=F𝒟+​(n,c)C𝒟​(n).\lim_{\alpha\to\infty}\bm{\omega}^{\mathrm{new}}_{n,c}=\frac{F_{\mathcal{D}}^{+}(n,c)}{C_{\mathcal{D}}(n)}. (25)

This is the EM update obtained by normalizing the expected edge counts (Peharz et al., 2020). Thus, full-batch EM is recovered as a limit of the additive update, rather than generally at a finite learning rate.

Interpolated mini-batch EM.

For CB​(n)>0C_{\mathrm{B}}(n)>0, choose Tn,c=1/CB​(n)T_{n,c}=1/C_{\mathrm{B}}(n) for every child cc. Substituting into Equation 24 gives

𝝎n,cnew\displaystyle\bm{\omega}^{\mathrm{new}}_{n,c} =𝝎n,c+α​FB+​(n,c)/CB​(n)1+α\displaystyle=\frac{\bm{\omega}_{n,c}+\alpha F_{\mathrm{B}}^{+}(n,c)/C_{\mathrm{B}}(n)}{1+\alpha} (26)
=(1−λ)𝝎n,c+λFB+​(n,c)CB​(n),λ:=α1+α.\displaystyle=(1-\lambda)\bm{\omega}_{n,c}+\lambda\frac{F_{\mathrm{B}}^{+}(n,c)}{C_{\mathrm{B}}(n)},\qquad\lambda:=\frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha}.

This recovers the mini-batch interpolation rule of Peharz et al. (2020), with mixing coefficient 0≤λ<10\leq\lambda<1. The endpoint λ=1\lambda=1 corresponds to α→∞\alpha\to\infty.

Anemone.

Let ρn>0\rho_{n}>0 be the probability that a generative traversal of the current circuit reaches node nn. Choosing Tn,c=1/ρnT_{n,c}=1/\rho_{n} gives

𝝎n,cnew=ρn​𝝎n,c+α​FB+​(n,c)ρn+α​CB​(n),\bm{\omega}^{\mathrm{new}}_{n,c}=\frac{\rho_{n}\bm{\omega}_{n,c}+\alpha F_{\mathrm{B}}^{+}(n,c)}{\rho_{n}+\alpha C_{\mathrm{B}}(n)}, (27)

which is Anemone’s basic update (Liu et al., 2025b, Eq. (7)). Its effective step size depends on the node’s usage in the batch relative to its usage under the current model.

Rows with zero batch flow are left unchanged; unreachable nodes are also left unchanged. Nonnegative example weights, including w⁡(t)w(t), can be included in the average in Equation 23, yielding the corresponding weighted updates. These correspondences concern the basic updates without momentum or additional regularization. For our conditional objective, the positive statistic is replaced by FB+−FB−F_{\mathrm{B}}^{+}-F_{\mathrm{B}}^{-}; the dual-flow update addresses this signed case, with its properties proved in Appendix G.

Appendix G Proof of the Signed-Flow Update Properties

Proof of Proposition 3.1.

Fix an active sum node nn and abbreviate ωc:=ωn,c\omega_{c}:=\omega_{n,c}, ac:=Fℬ+​(n,c)a_{c}:=F_{\mathcal{B}}^{+}(n,c), bc:=Fℬ−​(n,c)b_{c}:=F_{\mathcal{B}}^{-}(n,c), and Tc:=T⁡(n,c)T_{c}:=T(n,c). All quantities are evaluated at the pre-update parameters and held fixed as α\alpha varies. The derivatives are taken with respect to directly parameterized, untied edge weights before enforcing row normalization; neural outputs and all other circuit inputs are held fixed. Define the unnormalized updated weights and their row normalizer as

uc​(α):=ωc​1+α​Tc​ac/ωc1+α​Tc​bc/ωc,S⁡(α):=∑cuc​(α).u_{c}(\alpha):=\omega_{c}\frac{1+\alpha T_{c}a_{c}/\omega_{c}}{1+\alpha T_{c}b_{c}/\omega_{c}},\qquad S(\alpha):=\sum_{c}u_{c}(\alpha). (28)

Then Equation 9 is precisely ωcnew=uc​(α)/S⁡(α)\omega_{c}^{\mathrm{new}}=u_{c}(\alpha)/S(\alpha).

(i) Positivity and normalization.

For every finite α≥0\alpha\geq 0, both terms 1+α​Tc​ac/ωc1+\alpha T_{c}a_{c}/\omega_{c} and 1+α​Tc​bc/ωc1+\alpha T_{c}b_{c}/\omega_{c} are finite and at least one. Thus uc​(α)>0u_{c}(\alpha)>0 and 0<S⁡(α)<∞0<S(\alpha)<\infty. Consequently, ωcnew>0\omega_{c}^{\mathrm{new}}>0 and ∑cωcnew=1\sum_{c}\omega_{c}^{\mathrm{new}}=1.

(ii) Recovery of the standard update.

Consider a smooth, decomposable standalone PC with normalized input distributions and every sum row normalized. Let ZZ be its unconditional normalizer, with all variables marginalized and no additional evidence factors. Let TD𝝎⁡(n)>0\operatorname{TD}_{\bm{\omega}}(n)>0 denote the probability that a generative traversal of the current circuit visits sum node nn. Then, we can write ρn:=TD𝝎⁡(n)>0\rho_{n}:=\operatorname{TD}_{\bm{\omega}}(n)>0 for the probability that a generative traversal reaches nn. Under the independent-edge derivative convention,

∂log⁡Z∂log⁡ωc=ρn​ωc.\frac{\partial\log Z}{\partial\log\omega_{c}}=\rho_{n}\omega_{c}. (29)

This identity is the normalizer derivative underlying the standard circuit update (Liu et al., 2025b). To see it directly, evaluate the circuit with all variables marginalized. Every node then has value one. Reverse differentiation gives sensitivity ρn\rho_{n} at node nn; the derivative with respect to its edge weight ωc\omega_{c} is therefore ρn\rho_{n} times the child value, namely ρn\rho_{n}. Multiplication by ωc/Z=ωc\omega_{c}/Z=\omega_{c} yields Equation 29. Although Z=1Z=1 at normalized parameters, independently perturbing an edge need not preserve normalization, so this derivative is generally nonzero.

For the weighted minibatch averages, let w¯ℬ:=|ℬ|−1​∑(t,𝒙0,𝒙t)∈ℬw⁡(t)\bar{w}_{\mathcal{B}}:=|\mathcal{B}|^{-1}\sum_{(t,\bm{x}_{0},\bm{x}_{t})\in\mathcal{B}}w(t). In the standalone setting the unconditional normalizer is the same for every example, giving bc=w¯ℬ​ρn​ωcb_{c}=\bar{w}_{\mathcal{B}}\rho_{n}\omega_{c}. ωcnew=ωc+α​ac/ρn1+α​∑dad/ρn=ρn​ωc+α​acρn+α​∑dad,\omega_{c}^{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{\omega_{c}+\alpha a_{c}/\rho_{n}}{1+\alpha\sum_{d}a_{d}/\rho_{n}}=\frac{\rho_{n}\omega_{c}+\alpha a_{c}}{\rho_{n}+\alpha\sum_{d}a_{d}}, (31)

which is Equation 8 with the positive flows aca_{c}. Here the standalone objective in Equation 8 is the average log circuit output, whose log-weight derivatives are aca_{c}.

(iii) Full-batch EM limit.

Under the conditions in (ii), let ℬ\mathcal{B} be the full training set and assume A:=∑dad>0A:=\sum_{d}a_{d}>0. Dividing the numerator and denominator of Equation 31 by α\alpha yields

limα→∞ωcnew=limα→∞ρn​ωc/α+acρn/α+A=acA.\lim_{\alpha\to\infty}\omega_{c}^{\mathrm{new}}=\lim_{\alpha\to\infty}\frac{\rho_{n}\omega_{c}/\alpha+a_{c}}{\rho_{n}/\alpha+A}=\frac{a_{c}}{A}. (32)

The aca_{c} are the corresponding weighted expected edge counts. Normalizing them maximizes the sum-node EM surrogate ∑cac​log⁡ωcnew\sum_{c}a_{c}\log\omega_{c}^{\mathrm{new}} subject to nonnegative weights summing to one, and therefore gives the full-batch EM update for the weighted objective. For unit example weights, this is ordinary full-batch EM. Zero counts may yield zero weights in this limit, which is consistent with strict positivity holding only for finite steps. If A=0A=0, all aca_{c} vanish and Equation 31 leaves the row unchanged; the normalized-count formula is not used in that case.
